title: Prince Salim Rebels Against Akbar
text:
The Mughal emperor Akbar long had no surviving son. According to tradition, he visited the Sufi saint Salim Chishti at Sikri to ask for his blessing, and when a son was born in 1569, he named him Salim after the saint and later built a new capital, Fatehpur Sikri, at the saint's village.

Salim was raised as heir, but as he grew older, his father lived on and showed no sign of handing over power. Salim drank heavily and grew impatient. In 1600, while Akbar was campaigning in the Deccan, Salim seized the fort at Allahabad and set up his own court there, behaving as an independent king.

The worst blow came in 1602. Akbar's closest friend and adviser, the historian Abul Fazl, was returning to court when he was ambushed and killed by a chieftain acting on Salim's orders. Akbar was devastated. Salim himself admitted the deed years later in his memoirs, saying he believed Abul Fazl was turning his father against him.

The women of the family worked to heal the breach. Akbar's senior wife, Salima Sultan Begum, went to Allahabad and brought Salim back to court, and father and son were reconciled, though further quarrels followed. When Akbar lay dying at Agra in October 1605, he recognized Salim as his heir. Salim took the throne as Jahangir.
lesson: A child's impatience for power can wound a parent deeply, yet families can still find their way back. Peacemakers within a family are often its unsung heroes.
people: Akbar, Salim (Jahangir), Abul Fazl, Salima Sultan Begum
source: Jahangir, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (Memoirs of Jahangir), trans. Rogers and Beveridge; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama
